Rolling-window aggregates

Source: R/roll.R
roll.Rd

Compute a right-aligned rolling (moving) aggregate over a numeric vector: n-wide windows ending at (and including) each element. The leading n - 1 elements have no complete window and are always NA. Matches data.table::frollmean()/frollsum()/etc.'s own align = "right" default exactly (see Details).

Usage

roll_mean(x, n, na.rm = FALSE)

roll_sum(x, n, na.rm = FALSE)

roll_min(x, n, na.rm = FALSE)

roll_max(x, n, na.rm = FALSE)

roll_sd(x, n, na.rm = FALSE)

roll_median(x, n, na.rm = FALSE)

Arguments

x

A numeric vector.

n

A single positive whole number: the window width.

na.rm

Logical scalar, default FALSE. See Details.

Value

A numeric vector the same length as x.

Details

na.rm = FALSE (the default): any window containing at least one NA produces NA for that position ("NA poisoning"). na.rm = TRUE: a window is only ever NA because it doesn't yet have n physical elements available (the leading n - 1 positions, always). Once a window has n elements, NAs within it are dropped before computing (an all-NA window still yields NA). This na.rm = TRUE behavior was verified empirically against data.table::frollmean(x, n, na.rm = TRUE) (not assumed): the leading incomplete positions stay NA even though na.rm is set.

Inside mutate()/filter() on a tbl_gpu, roll_mean()/roll_sum()/ roll_min()/roll_max()/roll_sd() (not roll_median(), see below) run GPU-natively, in time that does not depend on the window width (segmented scans; cudf's own rolling kernel is kept for narrow windows, where it is faster, and for min/max of timestamps and logicals) – these R implementations are the CPU semantics reference and the engine for standalone use. cudf 25.12 has no MEDIAN rolling aggregation, so roll_median() always runs on the CPU (see "Median engines"). data.table::frollmean(x, n) (and its five siblings) work as equivalent GPU-native aliases inside mutate()/filter() too, as long as align/fill/adaptive are left at their defaults ("right", NA, FALSE) – any other value falls back / errors, matching this task's explicit "right-aligned only" scope.

Median engines. By default roll_median() uses a built-in exact engine that returns exactly stats::median() of each window converted to double (so integer and logical input give double, as median() of the window cast to double would): the same NA/na.rm handling, NaN treated as missing, Inf, and grouped windows. It runs in O(n log n) whatever the width (roughly 0.2 s per 1e6 rows). options(cuplyr.roll_median = "frollmedian") (or the environment variable CUPLYR_ROLL_MEDIAN; the option wins) opts in to data.table::frollmedian(), which needs data.table >= 1.18.4 (Suggests). Its result equals data.table::frollmedian(x, n, na.rm = na.rm) with NaN treated as NA first, except that every position where data.table returns Inf or -Inf takes the exact engine's value (so a midpoint of two finite values that overflows comes out finite, as in stats::median()). Everywhere else it can differ from stats::median() by one rounding step (1 ulp) on windows with an even number of non-missing values. It is faster on wide windows without NAs, but slower than the default with NAs and na.rm = TRUE on wide windows (about 4x slower at width 1001 with 1% NA) and on thousands of small groups (several times slower). If it is requested but data.table is missing or too old, the exact engine is used and a message says so once per session. Any other value of the option warns once (class cuplyr_warning_invalid_option) and the exact engine is used; see cuplyr-options. data.table::frollmedian() written inside mutate() keeps data.table's own result.

The internal option cuplyr.roll_path (else the environment variable CUPLYR_ROLL_PATH), one of "auto" (the default), "scans" or "cudf", forces one of the two GPU paths. It exists for tests and benchmarks and changes speed, not results.
